cards.q: Give the physical state and colour of each halogen, fluorine to iodine, at room temperature.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{F_{2}}\): pale yellow gas.
\(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\): pale green gas.
\(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\): red-brown liquid.
\(\mathrm{I_{2}}\): grey-black solid (gives a purple vapour).
cards.why: The states change from gas to liquid to solid down the group because the melting and boiling temperatures increase.

cards.q: State the trend in boiling temperature of the halogens down Group 7.
cards.a: Boiling temperature increases down the group.
cards.why: Fluorine and chlorine boil below room temperature, bromine just above it, and iodine is a solid at room temperature.

cards.q: Explain why the boiling temperature of the halogens increases down the group.
cards.a: The molecules get larger, so the London (van der Waals) forces between them get stronger.
marks: Halogens are simple molecules, \(\mathrm{X_{2}}\), held together by London (van der Waals) forces between the molecules.
Down the group the molecules have more electrons (and are larger).
So the London forces between molecules are stronger.
More energy is needed to overcome these forces, so the boiling temperature is higher.

cards.q: True or false: iodine has a higher boiling temperature than chlorine because the \(\mathrm{I{-}I}\) covalent bond is stronger than the \(\mathrm{Cl{-}Cl}\) bond.
cards.a: False. Boiling overcomes the forces between molecules, not the covalent bond. (The \(\mathrm{I{-}I}\) bond is in fact weaker.)
cards.why: Iodine has stronger London forces between its molecules because each molecule has more electrons.

cards.q: Define electronegativity.
cards.a: The power of an atom to attract the pair of electrons in a covalent bond.
cards.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative element of all.

cards.q: Explain the trend in electronegativity down Group 7.
cards.a: Electronegativity decreases down the group.
marks: Electronegativity decreases down the group.
The atoms have more electron shells, so the atomic radius increases.
The bonding pair of electrons is further from the nucleus (and more shielded by inner electrons).
So the attraction between the nucleus and the bonding pair is weaker, despite the greater nuclear charge.

cards.q: True or false: iodine is more electronegative than chlorine because its nucleus contains more protons.
cards.a: False. Iodine is less electronegative than chlorine.
cards.why: The extra protons are outweighed by the extra shells: the bonding pair is further away and more shielded.

cards.q: State the trend in oxidising ability of the halogens down Group 7.
cards.a: Oxidising ability decreases down the group: \(\mathrm{F_{2} > Cl_{2} > Br_{2} > I_{2}}\).
cards.why: A halogen acts as an oxidising agent by gaining electrons, and this gets harder down the group.

cards.q: Explain why the halogens become less reactive (weaker oxidising agents) down the group.
cards.a: The atoms are larger, so they attract an extra electron less strongly.
marks: A halogen reacts by gaining an electron (it is reduced).
Down the group the atomic radius increases and there is more shielding.
So the attraction between the nucleus and an incoming electron is weaker.
So the halogen gains electrons less readily: it is a weaker oxidising agent.

cards.q: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of chlorine with aqueous potassium bromide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}(aq) + 2Br^{-}(aq) \rightarrow 2Cl^{-}(aq) + Br_{2}(aq)}\)
cards.why: Chlorine is the stronger oxidising agent, so it oxidises bromide ions to bromine. The solution turns from colourless to orange (yellow).

cards.q: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of bromine water with aqueous sodium iodide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Br_{2}(aq) + 2I^{-}(aq) \rightarrow 2Br^{-}(aq) + I_{2}(aq)}\)
cards.why: The solution turns brown as iodine forms.

cards.q: Which of these mixtures react? \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\) + \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\); \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\) + \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\); \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) + \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\); \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\) + \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\).
cards.a: Only \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + I^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{Br_{2} + I^{-}}\) react.
cards.why: A halogen displaces (oxidises) only the halide ions of halogens below it in the group.

cards.q: Give the colours of chlorine, bromine and iodine in aqueous solution and in a non-polar organic solvent such as cyclohexane.
cards.a:
Water: \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\) pale green (almost colourless), \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\) orange (yellow), \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) brown.
Cyclohexane: \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\) pale green (almost colourless), \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\) orange (red-orange), \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) purple (violet).
cards.why: Dilute bromine and iodine solutions can both look yellow-brown in water; in the organic layer they are easy to tell apart.

cards.q: In a halogen displacement experiment, why is a non-polar organic solvent such as cyclohexane added and shaken with the aqueous mixture?
cards.a: To identify which halogen has formed: the colours in the organic layer are distinct.
marks: The halogens are non-polar, so they are more soluble in the organic solvent than in water.
The halogen moves into the organic (upper) layer.
In the organic layer iodine is purple and bromine is orange, which are easy to tell apart (in water both can look brown/yellow).

cards.q: True or false: in \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2Br^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-} + Br_{2}}\), the bromide ion is the oxidising agent.
cards.a: False. \(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\) is the oxidising agent (it is reduced, 0 to −1); \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\) is the reducing agent (it is oxidised, −1 to 0).
cards.why: The oxidising agent is the species that is itself reduced.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of sodium with chlorine, and give the change in oxidation number of each element.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{2Na(s) + Cl_{2}(g) \rightarrow 2NaCl(s)}\)
Na: 0 to +1 (oxidised). Cl: 0 to −1 (reduced).
cards.why: Chlorine is the oxidising agent: it gains the electrons that sodium loses.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of magnesium with bromine, and give the change in oxidation number of each element.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Mg(s) + Br_{2}(l) \rightarrow MgBr_{2}(s)}\)
Mg: 0 to +2 (oxidised). Br: 0 to −1 (reduced).
cards.why: Group 1 and Group 2 metals react in the same way with every halogen, forming ionic halides.

cards.q: State the trend in reducing ability of the halide ions.
cards.a: Reducing ability increases down the group: \(\mathrm{I^{-} > Br^{-} > Cl^{-} > F^{-}}\).
cards.why: A halide ion acts as a reducing agent by losing an electron.

cards.q: Explain why iodide ions are stronger reducing agents than chloride ions.
cards.a: The iodide ion is larger, so its outer electrons are lost more easily.
marks: \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\) is larger than \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) (more electron shells).
Its outer electrons are further from the nucleus and more shielded.
So they are less strongly attracted and more easily lost (given to another species).

cards.q: Write the equation and give the observation for the reaction of solid sodium chloride with concentrated sulfuric acid.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{NaCl(s) + H_{2}SO_{4}(l) \rightarrow NaHSO_{4}(s) + HCl(g)}\)
Observation: steamy (misty) white fumes of \(\mathrm{HCl}\).
cards.why: This is an acid–base reaction only: \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) is too weak a reducing agent to reduce sulfuric acid.

cards.q: What would you observe when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium bromide?
cards.a: Steamy fumes (\(\mathrm{HBr}\)), orange-brown fumes (\(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\)) and a colourless gas with a choking smell (\(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\)).
cards.why: First \(\mathrm{HBr}\) forms; then bromide reduces some of the sulfuric acid to \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) and is itself oxidised to \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\).

cards.q: Write the redox equation for the reaction of hydrogen bromide with concentrated sulfuric acid. Give the change in oxidation number of sulfur.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{2HBr + H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow Br_{2} + SO_{2} + 2H_{2}O}\)
Sulfur: +6 to +4.
cards.why: Bromine is oxidised from −1 to 0. \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) is the reduction product.

cards.q: What would you observe when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium iodide?
cards.a: Steamy fumes (\(\mathrm{HI}\)), purple fumes or a black solid (\(\mathrm{I_{2}}\)), a yellow solid (\(\mathrm{S}\)) and a smell of bad eggs (\(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\)).
cards.why: Iodide is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce sulfuric acid to \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\), \(\mathrm{S}\) and \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\).

cards.q: Write an ionic equation for the reduction of sulfuric acid to hydrogen sulfide by iodide ions.
cards.why: Sulfur goes from +6 to −2, gaining 8 electrons, so 8 iodide ions are oxidised. Equally valid: \(\mathrm{8HI + H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow 4I_{2} + H_{2}S + 4H_{2}O}\).

cards.q: Write an equation for the reduction of sulfuric acid to sulfur by hydrogen iodide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{6HI + H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow 3I_{2} + S + 4H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Sulfur goes from +6 to 0, gaining 6 electrons, so 6 iodide ions are oxidised.

cards.q: Give the oxidation number of sulfur in each reduction product of sulfuric acid formed with sodium iodide: \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\), \(\mathrm{S}\) and \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\).
cards.why: The further sulfur is reduced, the stronger the reducing agent must be: only iodide gets it to −2.

cards.q: Explain the different products formed when concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid NaCl, NaBr and NaI.
cards.a: The halide ions are increasingly strong reducing agents down the group, so they reduce sulfuric acid further.
marks: All three form the hydrogen halide (steamy fumes) in an acid–base reaction.
\(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) is too weak a reducing agent to reduce \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\): only \(\mathrm{HCl}\) forms.
\(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\) reduces \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\) to \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) (S +6 to +4), forming \(\mathrm{Br_{2}}\).
\(\mathrm{I^{-}}\) reduces \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\) to \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\), \(\mathrm{S}\) and \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\) (S as low as −2), forming \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\).
Reducing power increases down the group because the ions are larger and lose electrons more easily.

cards.q: True or false: when concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with sodium chloride, the chloride ion is oxidised.
cards.a: False. No redox takes place: \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\) simply donates a proton to \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\), forming \(\mathrm{HCl}\).
cards.why: Chlorine stays at −1. Only bromide and iodide are oxidised by concentrated sulfuric acid.

cards.q: Describe how to test a solution for halide ions, and give the result for chloride, bromide and iodide.
cards.a:
Add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution.
\(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\): white precipitate.
\(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\): cream precipitate.
\(\mathrm{I^{-}}\): yellow precipitate.
cards.why: The precipitates are silver chloride, silver bromide and silver iodide.

cards.q: Write the ionic equation for the formation of the precipitate when silver nitrate is added to a solution of bromide ions.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq) + Br^{-}(aq) \rightarrow AgBr(s)}\)
cards.why: The nitrate and the metal ion are spectator ions. The precipitate is cream.

cards.q: In the test for halide ions, why is the solution first acidified with dilute nitric acid?
cards.a: To remove ions such as carbonate and hydroxide, which would also form a precipitate with silver ions.
marks: Nitric acid reacts with (removes) \(\mathrm{CO_{3}^{2-}}\) and \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) ions.
These would otherwise form precipitates with \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}}\) (silver carbonate, silver oxide) and give a false positive.

cards.q: True or false: the solution in the halide test can be acidified with dilute hydrochloric acid instead of nitric acid.
cards.a: False. Hydrochloric acid adds \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ions, which would give a white precipitate of \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) whatever halide was present.
cards.why: Nitric acid is used because silver nitrate is soluble: it adds no ion that silver precipitates.

cards.q: How do the silver halide precipitates behave with ammonia solution?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{AgCl}\): dissolves in dilute ammonia.
\(\mathrm{AgBr}\): dissolves only in concentrated ammonia.
\(\mathrm{AgI}\): does not dissolve, even in concentrated ammonia.
cards.why: Solubility of the silver halides in ammonia decreases from chloride to iodide.

cards.q: Why is ammonia solution added after silver nitrate in the test for halide ions?
cards.a: To confirm which halide is present, because the white, cream and yellow colours can be hard to tell apart.
marks: The colours of the precipitates are similar and hard to distinguish by eye.
The silver halides differ in solubility in ammonia: AgCl dissolves in dilute, AgBr only in concentrated, AgI not at all.
So the ammonia result identifies the halide.

cards.q: Write an equation for silver chloride dissolving in ammonia solution.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{AgCl(s) + 2NH_{3}(aq) \rightarrow [Ag(NH_{3})_{2}]^{+}(aq) + Cl^{-}(aq)}\)
cards.why: The soluble diamminesilver(I) complex forms, so the precipitate dissolves.

cards.q: True or false: fluoride ions give a precipitate with acidified silver nitrate, like the other halide ions.
cards.a: False. Silver fluoride is soluble, so no precipitate forms.
cards.why: So a negative silver nitrate test does not rule out fluoride ions.

cards.q: What is a disproportionation reaction?
cards.a: A reaction in which the same element is simultaneously oxidised and reduced.
cards.why: Chlorine does this with water and with alkali: some Cl atoms go up in oxidation number and some go down.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of chlorine with water and give the oxidation number of chlorine in each species.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons HCl + HClO}\)
\(\mathrm{Cl_{2}}\): 0. \(\mathrm{HCl}\): −1. \(\mathrm{HClO}\) (chloric(I) acid): +1.
cards.why: Chlorine is both reduced and oxidised: a disproportionation. The products can also be written as ions: \(\mathrm{2H^{+} + Cl^{-} + ClO^{-}}\).

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of chlorine with water in bright sunlight.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{2Cl_{2} + 2H_{2}O \rightarrow 4HCl + O_{2}}\)
cards.why: Chlorine is reduced to chloride ions and oxygen is oxidised from −2 to 0. Chlorine water loses its chlorine faster in sunlight.

cards.q: Explain why chlorine is added to drinking water even though chlorine is toxic.
cards.a: It kills disease-causing bacteria, and at the low concentrations used the health benefits outweigh the risks.
marks: Chlorine (as chloric(I) acid, \(\mathrm{HClO}\), and \(\mathrm{ClO^{-}}\) ions) kills bacteria in water.
This prevents water-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid.
Chlorine is toxic, but it is used in very low concentrations.
So the benefit to health outweighs the risk of its toxic effects.

cards.q: Give arguments for and against adding chemicals such as chlorine or fluoride to public water supplies.
cards.a:
For: chlorine kills bacteria; fluoride reduces tooth decay; everyone benefits, including people who cannot afford other treatment.
Against: people cannot choose whether to take the chemical; chlorine is toxic and can react with organic matter to form harmful chlorinated compounds; too much fluoride can harm teeth and bones.
cards.why: Society weighs the advantages and disadvantages before deciding what is added to water supplies.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of chlorine with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide, and give a use of the solution formed.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + NaClO + H_{2}O}\)
Use: bleach (also a disinfectant, for example to clean surfaces and treat water).
cards.why: Sodium chlorate(I), \(\mathrm{NaClO}\), is the active ingredient in household bleach.

cards.q: Use oxidation numbers to show that \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + NaClO + H_{2}O}\) is a disproportionation.
cards.a: Chlorine goes from 0 to −1 (reduced) in \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) and from 0 to +1 (oxidised) in \(\mathrm{NaClO}\).
steps: The same element is both oxidised and reduced, so this is a disproportionation.

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of chlorine with hot, concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{3Cl_{2} + 6NaOH \rightarrow 5NaCl + NaClO_{3} + 3H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Chlorine disproportionates from 0 to −1 (in \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)) and to +5 (in sodium chlorate(V), \(\mathrm{NaClO_{3}}\)).

cards.q: Show that the reaction \(\mathrm{3Cl_{2} + 6NaOH \rightarrow 5NaCl + NaClO_{3} + 3H_{2}O}\) balances in terms of electrons transferred.
cards.a: Five Cl atoms each gain 1 electron (5 gained); one Cl atom loses 5 electrons (5 lost).
steps: One Cl: 0 to +5, so 5 electrons lost.
Five Cl: 0 to −1, so \(5 \times 1 = 5\) electrons gained.
Electrons lost equal electrons gained, so 5 : 1 is the ratio of chloride to chlorate(V).

cards.q: Predict the equation for the reaction of bromine with cold, dilute aqueous sodium hydroxide.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{Br_{2} + 2NaOH \rightarrow NaBr + NaBrO + H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: It is analogous to chlorine: bromine disproportionates from 0 to −1 (bromide) and +1 (bromate(I)).

cards.q: Write the equation for the reaction of hydrogen chloride gas with ammonia gas, and give the observation.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{NH_{3}(g) + HCl(g) \rightarrow NH_{4}Cl(s)}\)
Observation: dense white smoke.
cards.why: The white smoke is fine particles of solid ammonium chloride. This is also a test for \(\mathrm{HCl}\) (or for \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\)).

cards.q: Write the equation for hydrogen chloride dissolving in water.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{HCl(g) + H_{2}O(l) \rightarrow H_{3}O^{+}(aq) + Cl^{-}(aq)}\)
cards.why: Hydrogen halides donate a proton to water, forming strong acids. In moist air they form steamy fumes.

cards.q: Give the order of reducing power of the hydrogen halides HCl, HBr and HI, and the evidence for it.
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{HI > HBr > HCl}\).
Evidence: with concentrated sulfuric acid, \(\mathrm{HCl}\) does not react, \(\mathrm{HBr}\) reduces it to \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\), and \(\mathrm{HI}\) reduces it as far as \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\).
cards.why: The larger the halide, the more easily it gives up electrons.

cards.q: Use Group 7 trends to predict the appearance, oxidising power and halide-ion behaviour of astatine.
cards.a: A black solid; the weakest oxidising agent in the group; \(\mathrm{At^{-}}\) the strongest reducing agent of the halide ions.
cards.why: Astatine is below iodine, so it continues every trend: darker colour, higher melting temperature, lower reactivity.

cards.q: Predict what is seen when acidified silver nitrate and then concentrated ammonia are added to a solution of astatide ions.
cards.a: A precipitate (yellow or darker) of \(\mathrm{AgAt}\) that does not dissolve in concentrated ammonia.
cards.why: Silver halide solubility in ammonia decreases down the group, and AgI is already insoluble in concentrated ammonia.

cards.q: Predict the products when concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium fluoride, and explain.
cards.a: Only \(\mathrm{HF}\) (and \(\mathrm{NaHSO_{4}}\)): \(\mathrm{NaF + H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow NaHSO_{4} + HF}\).
cards.why: \(\mathrm{F^{-}}\) is an even weaker reducing agent than \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\), so it cannot reduce sulfuric acid.

cards.q: Predict, from Group 7 trends, how fluorine compares with the other halogens as an oxidising agent, and why.
cards.a: Fluorine is the strongest oxidising agent (the most reactive halogen).
cards.why: It has the smallest atoms, so an incoming electron is closest to the nucleus and least shielded.
